title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
description: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.L
body: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery."The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.""I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off."I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external. A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics"."We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

schema.headline: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis

title: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes
description: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days l
body: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze."We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California. Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured"."So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

schema.headline: Palisades fire: Man guilty of starting one of California's deadliest blazes

title: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'
description: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he
body: Robins, best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story"."It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm. "Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it."It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.Robins also hopes to raise the question - "do ghosts exist?", sparking the debate between belief and scepticism."What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy, who recently starred in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."Robins said The Witch Farm was "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in its creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from 22 November

schema.headline: The Witch Farm: Danny Robins drama inspired by 'real-life ghost story'

title: Mykhailo Mudryk accuses Andriy Shevchenko of lying about drugs test claims
description: Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his disp
body: Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it."My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk. "In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'."Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong."Mudryk also said the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

schema.headline: Mykhailo Mudryk accuses Andriy Shevchenko of lying about drugs test claims

title: Ed Miliband: EU deal not dependent on tuition fees agreement
description: A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuitio
body: A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees."President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely.""The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget. He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively"."Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU."A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations. She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

schema.headline: Ed Miliband: EU deal not dependent on tuition fees agreement

title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
description: A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are cont
body: A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height. For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction."They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change."They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers."How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used."The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

schema.headline: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm

title: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop
description: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being
body: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.Their firm, Libre By Nexus,  which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable. In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company."I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.  "I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund.  A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company. Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation."Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed."But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss"."The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention.  "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

schema.headline: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop

title: Sandpaper scandal: Darren Lehmann again denies knowing of plot while Australia coach
description: Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann has again vehemently denied any knowledge of the sandpaper plot, despite detailed allegations from Cameron Bancr
body: Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann has again vehemently denied any knowledge of the sandpaper plot, despite detailed allegations from Cameron Bancroft.In an ongoing row about the cheating scandal that took place in Australia's third Test against South Africa in 2018, Bancroft published a testimony running to more than 4,000 words in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday.At the same time, Lehmann was commentating on Australia's third one-day international against England, with Bancroft's account prompting him to leave the match early.On Saturday, Lehmann returned to broadcast for the BBC and Australian network ABC on the first T20 international in Melbourne.In an extended and emotional interview, addressing a range of Bancroft's claims, Lehmann said:He "didn't know" sandpaper was used by his Australia team.No coaches encouraged players to tamper with the ball before or during Australia's tour of South Africa in 2018.He is "not sure" about a walkie-talkie conversation with 12th man Peter Handscomb, which Bancroft claimed was an instruction from Lehmann to remove the sandpaper from the field.He resigned as Australia coach before he was sacked and did not sign a non-disclosure agreement.The fallout from the sandpaper scandal took him to a "really dark place".Lehmann's renewed denial came on the same day Cricket Australia confirmed its "unanimous support" for Pat Cummins as Australia captain.Earlier, Cummins' fellow fast bowler Josh Hazlewood said he would consider his international future if the captain was forced to stand down.The debate about the sandpaper plot of 2018 was reopened two weeks ago by allegations in the autobiography of Usman Khawaja, who was part of the Australia team in Cape Town eight years ago.Khawaja's assertions that the whole team knew and should have taken responsibility have been supported by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland, who were all on the tour.Warner, former captain Steve Smith and Bancroft were the only players punished for the cheating plot. It was Bancroft's testimony that heaped pressure on Lehmann, Cummins and the other members of the Australia team who played at Newlands.Cummins, Hazlewood and the rest of the Australia bowlers who played in Cape Town have always denied knowledge or involvement in the plan to use sandpaper on the ball.Lehmann resigned as coach in the immediate aftermath of the South Africa tour, but the former Australia batter has always maintained his innocence."Sandpaper, I didn't know," he said on Saturday. "Obviously, it was used."The biggest thing with ball-tampering is it was just a bad time. Everyone, we all made mistakes."But you've just got to try and move on. I know it's hard for everyone. The game of cricket is bigger than any individual team. We're custodians of the baggy green and we got a few things wrong."Bancroft was caught on camera during the third Test, yet alleged the use of sandpaper had begun during the second Test.In Cape Town, TV footage showed Bancroft hiding the sandpaper in his trousers. In his account, Bancroft alleged Lehmann immediately told Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now".Responding to that allegation, Lehmann said: "I'm not sure. That was all after the fact. It was already played out on TV."That's Cameron's take on it. I'm not going to talk about him, but my view is different."In his version, Khawaja said players were encouraged before the South Africa series to get the ball swinging by any means necessary. Both Khawaja and Bancroft agreed players were further emboldened to cheat by coaches during the tour.Bancroft elaborated further, saying the whole playing squad and coaches openly discussed and even celebrated the effect of sandpaper during the second Test.Lehmann said: "No, I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement. I didn't get that question posed to me."I can't comment for anyone else. Again, because I said before, I can only comment on what I know."Bancroft said the sandpaper idea was thought up by Warner at tea on the second day of the second Test.Lehmann said: "I can't remember that conversation. Again, eight and a half years ago. You'd have to ask those people."That's the issue. I have my version and that's where I stand."Lehmann is currently head coach of Northamptonshire. In 2020, two years after the sandpaper saga, he had heart bypass surgery after falling ill on his 50th birthday.'I went to a really dark place'Lehmann was asked by ABC's Matt Clinch about the physical and mental toll of the sandpaper saga. The full answers are below:I mean, I can tell you this. Eight and a half years ago, and I don't like talking about this sort of scenario, but I went to a really dark place. As dark a place as you can think about.It took me, and this is just me, probably three or four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.To the stage where we are now, I'm not going back to that. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.There's things I remember and don't remember. It's eight and a half years ago. It was a traumatic time, none more so for my family.Without the support of family and friends back then, I don't know where I'd be.And that's the same with the family and friends, and even Northamptonshire this year, who've been a second family over the last three or four years. They've been outstanding.The support and messages I've got in the last few days have been something that's kept me reasonable.Mate, I don't want to go back to that.I feel for everyone at the moment and their families. Social media has been so vitriolic. The hatred is there. It's just unbelievable.I've never seen anything like it since 2018. And the trauma for everyone is there to see again.I know people aren't in a great place.For me, being one of them, you just try and contact as many people as you can, stay in touch with them and try and put one foot forward as best you can.Because it's not bloody easy, mate.Eight and a half years ago it was terrible for a lot of people. So to revisit where we are now is not great for a lot of people. That's sad.Clinch asked: "I don't want to ask you any inappropriate questions, but was that dark place a feeling of guilt over what you could have done differently?"Could have done a lot of things differently.I can only speak for me. I wish we did things differently and we didn't push the boundaries too far. We didn't get to the stage where we got to.I've just got to take responsibility for that. That's where I'm at.People will say X, Y and Z.We're talking about people's livelihoods and how they can move forward mentally, physically, be happy again.I want to see people be happy again. That doesn't look like we're there at the moment, does it?Some of the things that are being said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people.That's what I care about. I care about everyone. There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.Yes, there were mistakes. You apologise as best you can, you try and move on. That's sort of where I'm at, mate.Again, I'm not going back to that place. I don't want to.It feels like everyone's pushing you on to these bad places.Some of my colleagues with ABC and some other friendly journalists have checked in, which I really appreciate.But then you have people who haven't checked in who you thought would have. And then people making comments on you when they don't even know you for a start.It hurts your families more. The families are the bigger picture in all this.It's a big game and they do as many jobs as they can [unclear].I think the way the team's evolved, and I think they've been to these press conferences and evolved, they're happy where they are and they've worked hard on everything to be the best they can be.And that goes for a lot of people. That goes for me eight and a half years ago, that person I don't want to go back to, to this person now.I hope people respect that as best they can. I hope you respect that.I hope people can respect that everyone's going through a tough time and we just let the players play the game of cricket.Because it's a wonderful game being played and I love seeing, walking around the parks and seeing the boys and girls trying to represent the baggy green.We're only custodians of it.

title: Donating kidney to daughter a 'no-brainer', says Derby dad
description: Walker said Noa-Rae was a healthy child until he noticed her face becoming swollen at the age of two."It all started when she was quite young," he sai
body: Walker said Noa-Rae was a healthy child until he noticed her face becoming swollen at the age of two."It all started when she was quite young," he said. "She would wake up with a swollen face that would last for hours."We took her to the doctors and they originally thought she had a skin or eye problem, but we did a blood test and the results came back saying she had nephrotic syndrome."NHS England says nephrotic syndrome causes the kidneys to leak large amounts of protein into the urine, which reduces the amount of protein in your blood.The condition can lead to the "swelling of body tissues, a greater chance of catching infections and blood clots", the NHS said.It can be detected through a urine or blood test."At the time, me and my wife had no idea what nephrotic syndrome was because it's such a rare condition," said Walker."It's quite hard because you go from living a normal life to having multiple days and weeks in and around hospital."Walker said his daughter's kidneys were removed when she was three due to the severity of the condition.Noa-Rae then began dialysis, causing her to miss school and other day-to-day activities as she spent much of her time in hospital."She's been an absolute trooper, all she really knows is hospital appointments," said Walker.After having her kidneys removed, Walker said the next step "was always going to be a transplant"."Doctors mentioned that the parents would have quite a high chance of being a match," he said. "I think any parent in their right mind would think straight forward to helping out their kids. "To sacrifice one part of yourself to better your own kid's life should be a no-brainer really."NHS Blood and Transplant says kidneys may be rejected by the body when its immune system recognises the kidney has come from a different person and thinks it is not supposed to be there.But, doctors said they hoped Walker's kidney would keep working until Noa-Rae is "at least the age of 16".He said organ transplant and donation was "super important" and was urging other people to consider being a donor."It'll make a massive difference to whoever it needs to go to," said Walker."It could last one day, it could last years, but as long as she keeps getting them, she could live as much of a normal life as possible."NHS Blood and Transplant said 539 people in the East Midlands were on the kidney transplant waiting list at the end of October.Between April 2025 and March 2026, 196 kidney transplants were carried out in the region, including 141 from deceased donors and 55 from living donors. A total of 158 people donated a kidney in the past year with 108 deceased donors and 50 living donors.Walker said his family were now looking forward to life beyond hospital appointments and treatment."There should hopefully be a bit less hospital time," he said."She will still have check-ups once a week, which will slow down to once a month and progressively even less."She'll be at school full-time, which she really enjoys, so that'll be a good thing."

schema.headline: Donating kidney to daughter a 'no-brainer', says Derby dad

title: James Bond: Could Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney or Jodie Comer be the next Bond girl opposite Robert Pattinson?
description: After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?What’s clear is that Patt
body: After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they go for an equally big name as a ‘Bond girl’, or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya, whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.The duo have already shared three films together this year and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said, external.Other names that have been floated include Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley, Marisa Abela, Emily Blunt, Lily James, Chase Infiniti, Inde Navarrette, Simone Ashley, Deva Cassel and Ambika Mod.And it could easily be someone totally different. Producers have previously chosen a Bond girl who isn't particularly famous yet - or is on the cusp of stardom.Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007.Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money. "We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".Many people say, however, there is still further to go.Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see.""They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," suggests Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and filmmaker."I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour."No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds  entertainment journalist Caroline Frost. Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit"."Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

schema.headline: James Bond: Could Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney or Jodie Comer be the next Bond girl opposite Robert Pattinson?

title: Phoebe Bridgers: Fans use art to visualise phone-free concert era
description: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember themImage source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers' concerts
body: Phoebe Bridgers banned phones at her gigs, so fans are using art to remember themImage source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers' concerts have inspired some fans to explore their artistic talentByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatPhoebe Bridgers has drawn in fans over the years with her raw, vulnerable lyrics and indie sound that can make even the messiest emotions feel less lonely. The US artist's third album Lost Weekend, released this summer after a six-year wait, delves into falling in and out of love, grappling with change and the confusing feelings that come with grief.On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy - a move that's had an unexpected side effect.Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.Massive Bridgers fan Olivia MacDonald, from Massachusetts, attended the singer's show in Boston last month.She was initially "shocked" by the no-phone rule, as employed by artists including Bob Dylan and Jack White, but became a convert.Without the distraction of phones, she says, fans chatted, danced and sang along with each other."Once I got to the concert, I realised this is such a unique way to connect and bring everybody together," she says. Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Olivia MacDonaldImage caption, Fans have used a range of mediums to recreate moments from The Lost TourSlide 1 of 4, Hand drawn sketches by Olivia MacDonald. One page depicts eyes with blue tears streaming down. The other page has a drawing of a guitar. The words 'You're standing too close I can see brushstrokes' is written around the sketches., Fans have used a range of mediums to recreate moments from The Lost TourMacDonald, a pen and ink artist, brought her sketchbook along to the show after spotting fellow fans' interpretations on social media. She relived the gig by drawing standout moments such as Bridgers' dripping, electric blue eye make-up and her guitar, originally owned by the late American musician Elliott Smith."Everybody takes away something different," says 28-year-old MacDonald."That's the beauty of it, that everybody can have a different interpretation."Sharing her designs on social media helped her connect with other fans, who reached out to discuss their experiences of the show. "I feel like with photos or videos, you capture a moment in time, and with drawings, you really capture a feeling and people can connect to that feeling," she says."It sparks more conversation too." Image source, Olivia MacDonaldImage caption, Fan Olivia MacDonald has been converted by the no-phone ruleBridgers has navigated an emotional whirlwind since she was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged and critically acclaimed album Punisher in 2020.The 32-year-old Californian has toured and won three Grammys with supergroup Boygenius, lived out a high-profile romance and breakup with Irish actor Paul Mescal, and lost her dad in 2023.Fans believe she explores some of these experiences in her latest album. MacDonald says Bridgers explained to the Boston crowd that the no-phone rule would allow her to talk openly with her audience like friends, without the worry of those moments ending up online.Some fans expressed worries the policy could exclude people with disabilities or those who might need to contact someone in an emergency.MacDonald says she shared the reservations, but points out fans were able to keep their phones on them and access the sealed pouches they were stored in at special designated areas inside the venue.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Phoebe Bridgers was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged album Punisher in 2020Fan Anna Meyer, who attended the New York show, agrees the device-free aspect made the show a better experience for artist and audience, and allowed the special lighting effects to be fully appreciated without being distorted by phone lights.The graphic designer, 35, chose to capture this element afterwards - focusing on a poignant moment when a kneeling Bridgers played piano in the glow of a spotlight. "It was so cathartic to feel so inspired," she says."And I do wonder, if I did have my phone, would I have felt this need to sit down and immediately draw something from the show?"Meyer feels the trend is particularly special as it's put a focus on techniques, such as pen and paper, in an age when traditional art feels under threat. "We're now in an era of AI where they want us to believe if you want to create something visual, you have to use a computer and AI programme," she says."And it's just not true. "We all have the ability to create, and our own creations that come from our own mind and hand are far better than anything that a computer can create."And sometimes even far better than anything that a camera can capture."Figure caption, Phoebe Bridgers fan Anna Meyer's time-lapse of her artwork inspired by the singer's gig had a positive response onlineFollowers of the new trend argue it also helps to guard against gig spoilers, where big moments go viral on social media before crowds get to see them in-person.Lillie Collins, a fan from Michigan, feels artwork offers "a little teaser" rather than giving everything away. The 20-year-old painted her own interpretation after seeing Bridgers' show in  Detroit and her videos revealing the piece blew up on TikTok.She says the wave of positive responses was "very exciting" as she'd never had that reaction before, and it's now made her consider that creating art could be a successful career route.Bridgers herself appears to approve too, as her team has shared several posts praising the artworks, external. MacDonald and Meyer were among those who got shout-outs on the official Lost Tour Instagram page, as was Collins, who says the idea Bridgers may have seen her artwork had her "screaming"."I really appreciate how she was able to bring this level of creativity and humanity into her performances," she says. Image source, Lillie CollinsImage caption, Lillie Collins got a shout-out on the official Lost Tour Instagram pageBridgers will kick off her UK run of shows at Manchester's Co-op Live on Thursday, followed by dates in Glasgow, Birmingham and London.Ayanoh Nakamoto was one of the fans who attended a special intimate show at Union Chapel, London, where Bridgers tested the no-phone policy.She will be back in the crowd for the first London show next month, and says the "excitement has built up so much because we haven't been able to see what is really happening in the US right now". "It's just so cool to have an experience where it feels like it isn't spoilt for you," she says.Despite Nakamoto running a TikTok page where she shares her concert video content, she admits it feels liberating to put her phone away and be in the moment. She jokes she doesn't have an "artistic bone" in her body, but thinks this might be her chance to try her hand at drawing, even if it is a stick-figure sketch."I wonder if this is going to be a stepping stone for artists to maybe have this at more concerts and just feel that connection back to the audience in the future."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Phoebe Bridgers: Fans use art to visualise phone-free concert era

title: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
description: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of p
body: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.""Purebreds," says the woman filming.Warning: This story contains images some might find upsettingIn the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page."I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged."The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message."When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals.  "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila."So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths."Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.Or not, as the case may be.Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated."Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago."I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace."Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment."Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak"."I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says. "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN."Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said."To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more."We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.  "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

schema.headline: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: George Russell says 'somebody has to stand up to' Max Verstappen
description: 'Somebody has to stand up to that guy' - Verstappen-Russell rivalry blows up againImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Max Verstappen (left) and G
body: 'Somebody has to stand up to that guy' - Verstappen-Russell rivalry blows up againImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Max Verstappen (left) and George Russell (right) will start on the front row in the Las Vegas Grand PrixByF1 Correspondent in Las VegasThe Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy"."That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over."He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, George Russell and Max Verstappen battling for track position during final practice in Las VegasThese two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position. They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."Verstappen called Russell a "backstabber" and a "loser".That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour. Image source, EPAImage caption, Verstappen goes off track after clashing with Russell in Las VegasAll this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.Despite widespread disquiet about going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, everyone has been towing the party line on that one recently in public, that they trust governing body the FIA and Formula 1 to have made the right decision.After qualifying, though, Verstappen came close to becoming the first to break the omerta, when he told the Dutch media "of course I would rather be at home", before repeating that he trusted the sport's bosses on the matter.BBC Sport has been told of at least one other major driver who would rather not be going to the Middle East specifically because of concerns about safety.As for the racing here in Sin City, it is set up beautifully.The two drivers on the front row, as well as not troubling to hide their distaste for each other, are also the only two to have won here.Verstappen has won two of the three events on the Strip circuit, sandwiching Russell's victory in 2024.In theory, that could give an opportunity to McLaren's Lando Norris, who qualified fourth, and starts third as a result of Antonelli's penalty.But the 2025 world champion was concerned about the McLaren's lack of straight-line speed."The pace in the car is not bad," he said. "The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we are not going to be able to overtake someone, so I think it's going to be a tough day."His team principal Andrea Stella was more optimistic.McLaren's battle with Red Bull for third in the constructors' championship - the two are separated by just 17 points - is one of the few major issues still to be settled this year.Stella saw the fact that Norris had missed out on beating Russell by just 0.02secs, despite having a plastic bag caught in his floor that he said had cost 0.1secs, as reason for optimism.As were the lessons of the Italian Grand Prix - held on a track with similarly long straights and big braking zones."We saw that because of this towing effect you actually can stay tangled, linked to the other cars," Stella said. "So we are definitely looking forward to tomorrow and encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive."Because the tow effect is so big and because it's bigger than Monza, racing will be difficult to predict."So we need to make sure that from a driver's team point of view, we are ready for all the situations."It's also a circuit that may offer quite a few safety cars, and will be interesting, for instance, restarting from safety car with a tyre warm-up. Definitely an interesting one to be part of and to follow."Las Vegas Grand PrixRace start at 04:00 GMT on SundayLive commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live with build-up from 03:30; live text updates on BBC Sport website and appLas Vegas GP starting grid after penalties1. title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
description: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're
body: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so."We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in."We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia."Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear."I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November."You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said."We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres. Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".Google has been contacted for comment.

schema.headline: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
